catalog_quote: [p.28, sec. 2.1.2.3] Stress is non-phonemic. The most pronounced stress occurs on the first syllable of words, except verbs where it may occur elsewhere. Unaffixed verb roots of tone Class I are stressed on the first syllable: pona 'to cut', waraa 'to touch', rumaa 'to portion out'. Affixation of tone Class I verbs causes stress to shift to final stem syllable. Tone Class I verb stems are stressed on the second syllable: ruba 'to throw away'. Three features of Kewa phonology produce a minor stress if they occur on unstressed syllables: (1) high tone, (2) fortis consonants and (3) /aa/. ... audit.reasoning: The classification (non-phonemic word-initial primary stress; second syllable in long noun stems; verb stress by tone class/affixation; 'minor stress' from high tone, fortis C, /aa/; lexical tone) rests on the primary descriptions of Kewa by Karl and Joice Franklin: the 1962/1965 phonology articles as reprinted in PL C-53 (1978) and the 1971 West Kewa reference grammar (PL C-16), both held as open sealang PDFs. I opened PL C-53 pdf pp.30, 40, 41, 49-50 and PL C-16 pdf p.23 and found every quoted passage verbatim at the stated printed pages; the Kewa II pages (1978:38) independently restate 'Nouns, pronouns, adjectives, and time words are stressed most frequently on the first syllable'. The newly downloaded 1969 ANU thesis (p.36) carries the identical West Kewa statement, and PL B-10 (1968) is silent on stress, reporting no East/West prosodic difference. sources.quote: 'The perceptual or auditory height of a tone may be conditioned by stress placement (Cf. Kewa I:35). Disregarding levels above the phonemic word, a primary stress occurs on the first syllable of any noun stem of less than four syllables and on the second syllable of any stem over four. Any basic low tone which occurs on such stressed syllables will be heard as mid.' Preface (p.iii) confirms the grammar describes West Kewa (fieldwork from 1967) while earlier published materials were East Kewa.
